etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English pecken, pekken, variant of Middle English piken, picken, pikken (“to pick, use a pointed implement”). More at pick.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To strike or pierce with the beak or bill (of a bird).

quote.citation: 1922 October 26, Virginia Woolf, chapter 2, in Jacob’s Room, Richmond, London:  […]  Leonard & Virginia Woolf at the Hogarth Press, →OCLC; republished London: The Hogarth Press, 1960, →OCLC:
quote.text: The rooster had been known to fly on her shoulder and peck her neck, so that now she carried a stick or took one of the children with her when she went to feed the fowls.

quote.citation: 1900 May 17, L[yman] Frank Baum, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chicago, Ill.; New York, N.Y.: Geo[rge] M[elvin] Hill Co., →OCLC:
quote.text: And the Wicked Witch said to the King Crow, "Fly at once to the strangers; peck out their eyes and tear them to pieces."

definitions.definition: (transitive) To form by striking with the beak or a pointed instrument.
To strike, pick, thrust against, or dig into, with a pointed instrument, especially with repeated quick movements.
To seize and pick up with the beak, or as if with the beak; to bite; to eat; often with up.

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Loues Labour’s Lost”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii]:
quote.text: This fellow pecks up wit as pigeons peas.

quote.citation: 1713 September 14, letter to Joseph Addison, The Guardian, issue 160.
quote.text: I HAVE laid a wager, with a friend of mine, about the pigeons that used to peck up the corn which belonged to the ants.

definitions.definition: To do something in small, intermittent pieces.
To type by searching for each key individually.

quote.citation: 1997 June 26, J. K. Rowling [pseudonym; Joanne Rowling], chapter 1, in Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone (Harry Potter; 1), London: Bloomsbury Publishing, →ISBN:
quote.text: At half past eight, Mr. Dursley picked up his briefcase, pecked Mrs. Dursley on the cheek, and tried to kiss Dudley good-bye but missed, because Dudley was now having a tantrum and throwing his cereal at the walls.

definitions.definition: An act of striking with a beak.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Probably from Anglo-Norman pek, pekke, of uncertain origin.

definitions.definition: One quarter of a bushel; a dry measure of eight quarts.

quote.citation: 1851, Henry Mayhew, “Gross Value of the Fruit and Vegetables Sold Annually in the London Streets”, in London Labour and the London Poor:
quote.text: 22,110 bushels of French beans, at 6d. per peck, or 2s. per bushel

quote.citation: 1851, Henry Mayhew, “Of the Experience of a Fried Fish-seller, and of the Class of Customers”, in London Labour and the London Poor:
quote.text: I took his advice, and went to Billingsgate for the first time in my life, and bought a peck of oysters for 2s. 6d.

definitions.definition: A great deal; a large or excessive quantity.

quote.citation: 1644, J[ohn] M[ilton], The Doctrine or Discipline of Divorce: […], 2nd edition, London: [s.n.], →OCLC, book:
quote.text: a peck of uncertainties and doubts

definitions.definition: To lurch forward; especially, of a horse, to stumble after hitting the ground with the toe instead of the flat of the foot.

quote.citation: 1928, Siegfried Sassoon, Memoirs of a Fox-Hunting Man, Penguin, published 2013, page 97:
quote.text: Anyhow, one of them fell, another one pecked badly, and Jerry disengaged himself from the group to scuttle up the short strip of meadow to win by a length.

definitions.definition: Discoloration caused by fungus growth or insects.

quote.citation: 1821, W. T. Moncrieff, Tom and Jerry:
quote.text: Gemmen, have you ordered the peck and booze for the evening?
